Effect of different aerobic hydrolysis time on the anaerobic digestion 
characteristics and energy consumption analysis

Keywords: 
Corn stover 
Aerobic hydrolysis 
Anaerobic digestion 
Methane production 
Energy consumption 
A B S T R A C T   
Aerobic hydrolysis of stover before anaerobic digestion is beneficial to improve the biodegradability of corn 
stover. Aerobic hydrolysis of corn stover at 43 ◦C was conducted to investigate the effects of hydrolysis time (0 h, 
8 h, 16 h, and 24 h) on the degradation of lignocellulose from corn stover and material conversion. Further 
anaerobic digestion and energy consumption analysis with the digestion temperature of 36 ◦C were carried out. 
The accumulation rate of volatile fatty acids began to slow down after 16 h of hydrolysis, and the concentration 
of acetic acid reached 221.85 mmol/L at 24 h of hydrolysis. The degradation rate of lignocellulose was obviously 
increased after hydrolysis. When the hydrolysis time was 16 h, it reached the maximum cumulative methane 
production with 268.75 ml/g VS. In terms of biogas production and energy conversion efficiency, it is more 
appropriate to choose 16 h as hydrolysis time in biogas engineering.

1. Introduction 
As a good fermentation material, crop stover has low sulfur content 
and high methane production, which is an important raw material 
source for the large-scale development of biogas engineering (Sun et al., 
2020b; Wang et al., 2019). In the production of biogas from corn stover 
(CS), due to the complex cross-linking structure of lignocellulose and the 
high crystallinity of cellulose molecules, it is difficult for the stover to be 
directly and efficiently degraded by microorganisms (Sun et al., 2018; 
Wainaina et al., 2020a). Therefore, improving the efficiency of hydro­
lysis and acidification of stover is the key factor to improve the biogas 
fermentation efficiency. In order to improve methane production in the 
fermentation process, it is necessary to pretreat CS properly. The pre­
treatment methods of CS can be roughly divided into physical, physical- 
chemical, chemical, and biological pretreatment, which have their own 
advantages and disadvantages (Wainaina et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 
2020). Most of the current researches are still in the small experiment 
stage with complicated process operation, which is difficult to apply in 
large-scale industrial production (Bremond et al., 2018; Yu et al., 2019; 
Wainaina et al., 2020b). Therefore, finding a pretreatment method with 
wide adaptability, strong operability, and low cost is still the focus and 
difficulty of research. 
Two-stage anaerobic digestion (AD) is a common type of anaerobic 
biological treatment process (Srisowmeya et al., 2020), which includes 
two parts: aerobic hydrolysis (AH) fermentation phase and anaerobic 
methanogenic fermentation phase. The AH stage mainly uses the action 
of aerobic microorganism and oxygen molecular to increase the degra­
dation rate of organic matter in the feed solution. In AD stage, metha­
nogens convert the small molecules in aerobic phase into methane. The 
microorganisms in the above-mentioned two stages are quite different, 
and each aerobic microorganism has its own specific object and suitable 
conditions. The reproductive capacity of aerobic microorganisms is 
much higher than that of anaerobic microorganisms, and lignin can be 
further degraded by microorganisms through the variation of side chain 
under the action of oxygen molecular (Li et al., 2018; Yang et al., 
2019b). 
AH technology is to decompose insoluble macromolecular organic 
matter into small molecular organic matter under the action of extra­
cellular enzymes, which provides substrate for subsequent fermentation 
bacteria (Du and Li, 2017; Kavitha et al., 2016; Schiltz et al., 2020). Lim 
et al. indicated that aerobic aeration in the AD system could improve the 
efficiency of hydrolysis and acidification, enhance the conversion of 
short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) to acetic acid, which was due to the 
enhancement of activities of acidogenic and hydrolytic bacteria and the 
slow degradation of compounds under micro-oxygen conditions (Lim 
and Wang, 2013; Wainaina et al., 2019). The suitable oxygen supply rate 
is the key factor to ensure the good effect of AD system (Park et al., 
2019). By controlling the intensity of aerobic aeration, the influence of 
excess oxygen on strictly anaerobic environment can be avoided. 
Moreover, the two-stage AD process can promote the stability of the 
system. Through the control of the acidogenic phase, balanced nutrition 
can be provided for the methanogenic phase, which avoids overload or 
inhibition of methanogenic phase (Shi et al., 2020). 
In the hydrolysis stage, it is the key problem to solve the high effi­
ciency AD of CS to destroy the lignin structure and make the extracel­
lular enzymes in contact with cellulose and hemicellulose (Awasthi 
et al., 2020; Wu et al., 2018). Ma et al. indicated that the degradation 
rates of lignin and hemicellulose could both reach more than 9% and 
28% after 24 h of hydrolysis, respectively (Ma et al., 2017; Wainaina 
et al., 2019). However, the changes of microbial species in the process of 
hydrolysis need to be further analyzed and discussed. Li et al. found that 
the average methane yield of the reactor after AH was 0.13 m3/kg 
(Volatile solids (VS)), which was significantly higher than that of the 
control group (Li and Pagilla, 2017). Similarly, De la Rubia et al. showed 
that in aerobic pretreatment experiments with different microorgan­
isms, the biogas production of olive oil plant wastewater treated with 
aspergillus was 35% higher than that of the control group (De la Rubia 
et al., 2018; Wainaina et al., 2019). From these studies, it can be seen 
that AH treatment has a positive effect on AD. In the current research, 
this treatment method is more applied to the treatment of wastewater 
pollutants, and the research on its application in AD of CS is still less. 
Moreover, the effect of AH time on AD characteristics and energy con­
sumption analysis of digestion system have not been explored, and AD 
efficiency is seriously restricted in cold regions of China by the long 
fermentation time of CS and the over degraded organic matter. 
In this study, the characteristics of AH of CS were explored, and the 
degradation of lignocellulose, the change of solid organic matter con­
tent, and material conversion were investigated. Then, the effects of 
different AH time on the AD performance of CS were analyzed, and the 
modified Gompertz model was used to predict the methane production 
potential. Moreover, based on the 100 m3 biogas engineering, the pro­
portion of net power consumption and energy conversion rate of AD 
system were studied, and the relationship between productivity and 
energy consumption in different AH time was analyzed. This study can 
provide important theoretical and practical value to the rapid degra­
dation and efficient utilization of CS and solve the problem of raw ma­
terial treatment in biogas engineering. 
2. Materials and methods 
2.1. Feed stocks and inoculum 
The CS was obtained in the Xiangyang Experimental Base of North­
east Agricultural University of Heilongjiang Province, China. The 
naturally dried CS was crushed by the hammer mill (Sida, China, 5.5 
kW) with the screen perforation of 5 mm. Inocula were obtained from 
the anaerobic digester of cattle manure at 35 ± 2 ◦C, and the size and 
hydraulic retention time (HRT) of digester were 5400 m3 and 30 d. 
Moreover, the detailed properties of CS and inocula were presented in 
Table 1. 
2.2. Experimental design 
The experiment was divided into two stages: AH and AD. According 
to the results obtained by the research group, 43 ◦C was selected as AH 
temperature in this experiment (Ma et al., 2017). A total of 21 jars with 
an effective volume of 1750 ml were prepared as the reactor in this 
experiment, and nine jars labeled from 1 to 9 were used in the AH stage 
to detect the changes of material composition in this process. Another 12 
jars labeled from 10 to 21 were used in the AD stage, four treatments 
with different hydrolysis time were CK (single AD without AH, jar 10 to 
12), hydrolysis for 8 h (Z43-8, jar 13 to 15), hydrolysis for 16 h (Z43-16, 
jar 16 to 18), and hydrolysis for 24 h (Z43-24, jar 19 to 21), respectively, 
and three parallel replicates were performed. 
Corn stover was mechanically crushed, and the TS and VS of the 
crushed stover and biogas slurry, and pH of the biogas slurry were 
measured. At the same time, part of the crushed CS and biogas slurry 
were stored in sealed bags and centrifugal tubes respectively for 
component detection. 80 g CS and 900 g inoculum (TS of reactants was 
8%) were loaded into each of above 21 jars, and one aeration device was 
put into each reactor except jar 10, 11, and 12. The aeration device 
adopted an electromagnetic vibration air pump, with 198 mm in length, 
145 mm in width, and 96 mm in height, and the aeration rate was set to 
2.5 L/ min. Each reactor was put into a 43 ◦C water bath for heating, and 
the aerator was turn on to start aeration. During the process of the re­
action, each reactor was stirred manually every 4 h, and samples were 
taken from jar 1 to 9 for the AH stage to be measured according to time 
changes. The sample was used for the detection and analysis of the 
components in the hydrolysis process, which included pH, TS, VS, 
lignocellulose, volatile fatty acids (volatile fatty acid), and infrared 
spectrum. 
The time of aerobic hydrolysis was controlled as a variable. The

aeration device in the jar 13 to 21 was taken out after the AH for 8 h, 16 
h, and 24 h, respectively, and then AD experiment was carried out in jar 
13 to 21. According to the results obtained by the research group, 36 ◦C 
was selected as AD temperature in this experiment (Ma et al., 2017; 
Yang et al., 2019a). The inoculation material was selected from the 
completely domesticated biogas slurry. The pH of the hydrolysate after 
AH was adjusted with the same amount of biogas slurry (the appropriate 
range was 6.5–7). Nitrogen was introduced to remove the oxygen in the 
hydrolysate, and the bottle mouth of the anaerobic reactor was sealed 
with rubber plug and glass glue. The reactor was connected with a 2 L air 
collecting bag and placed in 36 ◦C water bath for AD experiment. During 
the experiment, the air collecting bag was removed regularly every day 
to determine the gas composition and volume. Moreover, the fermen­
tation broth was manually shaken twice a day to make the raw materials 
fully contact with the microorganisms in the inoculum. 
2.3. Analytical methods 
The analysis of TS, VS, and pH was used the APHA Standard Method 
(Miner, 2006). Lignocellulose was determined through the Van Soest 
process by the fiber instrument (Ankom 200i, Anke Borui, Beijing, 
China), and correlative analysis procedure were as follows: analyzing 
the content of neutral detergent fiber, the content of acid detergent fiber, 
and the content of acid detergent lignin (Van Soest, 1967). Carbon (C) 
content and nitrogen (N) content were analyzed by the instrument of 
elemental analysis (EA 3000, LEEMAN, Beijing, China). Biogas and VFA 
were analyzed using the gas chromatography (GC-6890N, Agilent, USA). 
Biogas was determined through the thermal conductivity detector. VFA 
was determined through the flame ionization detector and capillary 
column. Each treatment was repeated three times. The functional groups 
were investigated using infrared spectrometer (TENSOR 27, Bruker Co., 
Ltd., Germany) with the temperature of 20 ◦C and the scanning range 
from 400 cm−1 to 4000−1.

2.5. Analysis of energy input and output 
Static energy consumption analysis method was used to study the 
energy consumption of biogas engineering, and the influence of aerobic 
pretreatment on energy consumption of AD system was investigated. 
The main accounting of energy consumption included raw materials 
crushing, feed solution warming, and heating energy consumption in 
hydrolysis and AD process to maintain normal operation of the system, 
and the energy consumption of mixing, material transportation and 
solid-liquid separation was not considered. The structure of biogas 
production system of two-phase AD in this study is shown in Fig. 1, and 
both the AH reactor and the AD reactor were 100 m3. The substrate was 
placed in the AH device in this system. The hydrolysis temperature was 
controlled to 43 ◦C by heating and heat preservation device. The AH 
device was equipped with self-priming centrifugal aeration device, with 
1050 mm in length, 840 mm in width, and 1100 mm in height, and the 
aeration rate was set to 4.95 m3/ min. The organic matter in the sub­
strate produced organic digestion liquid (acetic acid, propionic acid or 
butyric acid and other organic acids) under the action of hydrolysis 
bacteria and acid-producing bacteria. At the same time, the gas was 
released through the outlet of the AH device, and the organic digestion 
liquid was filtered by the perforated baffle and then pumped into the AD 
device with the circulating liquid. The heating device and the outer wall 
insulation layer in the AD device controlled the fermentation tempera­
ture at 36 ◦C, and the organic digestion liquid was converted into 
methane by methanogens in the AD device. For the biogas project, ac­
cording to the law of energy conservation, the heat loss of biogas project 
should be equal to the energy input from outside. The heat loss of biogas 
project mainly includes the heat required for the heating of new

2.5.2. Heating consumption of AD reactor 
Under the condition of constant temperature of feed solution in AD 
reactor, the heat balance equation of the reactor was shown as Eq. (5). 
Qhf + Qn + Qj = Qf + Qg + QW + Qc
(5)  
in which Qhf expresses the heat output of the heating system (kJ), Qn 
expresses the biochemical heat from the fermentation (kJ), Qj expresses 
the energy brought into the reactor by fermenting feed solution (kJ), Qf 
expresses the heat consumption of the reactor enclosure structure (KJ), 
Qg expresses the sensible heat loss from biogas exhausting reactor (KJ), 
QW expresses the heat loss of water evaporation in the reactor (KJ), and 
Qc expresses the energy brought out of the reactor by fermenting feed 
solution (kJ). 
In the actual biogas engineering, in order to keep the amount of feed 
solution in the reactor constant, the volume flow of feed solution 
entering and leaving the reactor is equal (Bayrakdar et al., 2016). Due to 
the temperature of the feed solution entering and leaving the reactor is 
the same, and the density and specific heat capacity of the feed solution 
before and after the AD reaction have little change, it can be concluded 
that Qj≈Qc. Considering that the activity of anaerobic microorganism is 
not strong enough and the heat released is very little, Qn can be ignored. 
Therefore, Eq. (5) can be simplified to Eq. (6). 
Qhf = Qf + Qg + QW
(6)

simplifications and assumptions are made. The reactor is a cylindrical

constant; the temperature of the wall in contact with the feed solution in 
the reactor is 36 ◦C; the temperature of the untouched wall is about

2.6. Data processing 
Three parallel replicates were performed in this study. Excel 2007 
was used for data collation, and Origin 8.5 software was employed for 
drawing. SPSS 22.0 software was used for one-way ANOVA to test the 
significance of the data and standardization of raw data. 
3. Results and discussion 
3.1. Analysis of parameters in aerobic hydrolysis 
After aerobic warming to 43 ◦C, the CS was further AH, and the 
variation of the VFA and pH in the 24 h hydrolysis were shown in Fig. 2 
(a). In the first 4 h, pH showed an upward trend, which was caused by 
the buffer material in the system maintaining the acid-base balance of 
the reactor, so that pH did not decrease with the rapid formation of 
organic acids (Zou et al., 2018). The optimum pH ranges of methanogens 
and hydrolytic acidification bacteria were not the same, and acidogenic 
bacteria could react at a lower pH. In this experiment, the pH value 
decreased rapidly from 6.92 to 5.86 within 4–8 h. Due to the rapid 
accumulation of VFA, the pH in the reactor began to decrease signifi­
cantly, and an environment suitable for the survival of acidogenic bac­
teria was gradually formed (Ma et al., 2017; Wainaina et al., 2020a). At 
the late stage of AH (after 20 h), pH showed a slight upward trend. The 
reason is that in the process of AH, in addition to sugars consumed by 
acidogenic bacteria to produce organic acids, proteins and other sub­
stances are also used by ammonifying bacteria, and gradually converted 
to NH4
+-N. The accumulation of ammonia substances made pH slightly 
higher in the later reaction period. 
Due to the high initial moisture, CS was soaked, dissolved or 
precipitated easily degradable part of matrix after AH. The cumulative 
content of acetic acid was the highest within 24 h. The cumulative 
content of ethanol increased at first and then decreased. The ethanol 
content rapidly increased to 93.18 mmol/L in the first 12 h before hy­
drolysis, and then decreased rapidly within 12 h to 24 h. The cumulative 
content of butyric acid increased rapidly from 10.31 mmol/L to 84.31 
mmol/L during 12 h to 24 h. The decreasing time of ethanol cumulative 
content and the increasing time of butyric acid cumulative content both 
started after 12 h, which was consistent with the change time of cu­
mulative content of acetic acid. This is because during the hydrolysis 
process, acetic acid was not only produced by the extracellular enzymes 
of acidogenic bacteria, but also by organic acids such as ethanol, pro­
pionic acid and butyric acid. Wang indicated that butyric acid was 
gradually converted to acetic acid, and the concentration of acetic acid 
went up (Wang et al. 2020c). After 8 h, with the continuous utilization of 
methanogens, the acetic acid concentration decreased, which was 
inconsistent with the results of this study. In this study, after 12 h, 
butyric acid content began to accumulate gradually, and ethanol content 
gradually decreased, which indicated that after hydrolysis to 12 h the 
production of acetic acid began to change from consuming butyric acid 
to ethanol. Organic acids are gradually metabolized by acetogenic 
bacteria during the reaction, which is also the reason why the concen­
tration of acetic acid was much higher than that of other organic acids 
during AH (Long et al., 2019; Wainaina et al., 2020b). 
The variation of lignocellulose degradation rate with AH time was 
shown in Fig. 2(b). After 4 h hydrolysis, the degradation rates of 
hemicellulose, cellulose, and lignin were 7.02%, 4.18%, and 3.33%, 
respectively. The warming energy of raw material came from the aerobic 
bacteria consuming the organic matter of CS and converting it into en­
ergy. After 24 h hydrolysis, the degradation rates of hemicellulose, 
cellulose, and lignin were 35.73%, 27.38%, and 8.06%, respectively. As 
the structure of CS was destroyed to some extent after AH, lignocellulose 
was consumed more. The variation of chemical composition and phys­
ical structure of CS can indirectly reflect the effect of AH (Sun et al., 
2018, 2020a). In the early stage of the reaction, the aerobic microor­
ganism made full use of oxygen. After 16 h, the product inhibition began 
to form gradually, which made the metabolic activity of microorganism 
begin to slow down and the consumption of oxygen began to weaken. At 
this time, oxygen molecules began to combine with lignin gradually, 
which showed the obvious degradation of lignin. 
It can be seen from figure that with the extension of hydrolysis time, 
CS all showed strong stretching band at 3400 cm−1 during hydrolysis. 
The O–H stretching band at 3400 cm−1 was weakened, which indicated 
that the hydrogen bond between cellulose molecules had been broken.

The absorption peak at 2925 cm−1 gradually decreased, which indicated 
that the aliphatic characteristics of decomposed CS decreased, and the 
extension of hydrolysis time accelerated the decomposition of carbo­
hydrates and aliphatic compounds. The absorption peak at 1731 cm−1 
disappeared after 8 h of hydrolysis, which illustrated that the ester bond 
formed by C = O of non-binding carbonyl carboxylate compounds in 
hemicellulose or lignin of CS disappeared. The absorption peaks at 1515 
cm−1 and 1427 cm−1 were N–H deformation vibration of phthalimide 
and stretching vibration peak of lignin aromatic ring C = C, and the 
strength of the two peaks was significantly reduced through hydrolysis. 
This is mainly due to the removal of some lignin by further AH. With the 
advance of hydrolysis time, the absorption peak at 1374 cm−1, 1245 
cm−1, and 1051 cm−1 decreased. 
The absorption peak of the acetyl ester bond at 1245 cm−1 dis­
appeared, mainly due to the decomposition of CS cellulose, which 
weakened its absorption intensity. The disappearance of the above peak 
after hydrolysis indicated that saponification destroyed part of the 
linkage between cellulose, hemicellulose, and lignin. It led to the release 
of part of cellulose and hemicellulose, the reduction of the steric hin­
drance between molecules, and increase of the porosity, which was 
beneficial for improving the fermentable performance of CS and pro­
moting the biogas production. Zhang studied the effect of aerobic 
deterioration on methane production through AD of CS silage following 
9 days air exposure of silage, and its effect of stover degradation was 
similar to the results of this study (Zhang et al., 2018). Therefore, AH can 
promote the decomposition of CS. 
3.2. Effect of aerobic hydrolysis time on methane production 
After charging and inoculation, all the reactors started smoothly and 
produced biogas normally. The AD experiment lasted for 26 d. At the 
end of the test, all treatments were close to stopping biogas production, 
and the pH after AD was in the range of 7.04–7.09. The cumulative 
methane production data in the test process were fitted using the first 
order model and modified Gompertz model for methane production. In 
the fitting process, the VS methane production rate (P∞) was used as 
evaluation indicators (Abreu et al., 2019; Wainaina et al., 2020a). 
The cumulative methane production and fitting curve of each 
treatment were shown in Fig. 3, and the fitting parameters of the 
equation were shown in Table 2. The R2 ranges of the first order model 
and Gompertz model were 0.979–0.985 and 0.997–0.999, respectively, 
which indicated that both models can simulate the cumulative methane 
production well, and the Gompertz model was more suitable for it. With 
the progress of AH, the cumulative methane production first increased 
and then decreased, which reached the maximum value at 16 h of hy­
drolysis with 268.75 ml/g VS. The reason is that during the hydrolysis 
process, the accumulation of soluble organic matter did not change 
much in 16–24 h. But easy to be used insoluble solid organic matter was 
still converted into CO2 and other substances through aerobic respira­
tion during this period, which made the substrate used for methane 
production lose, thus reducing the methane production efficiency of the 
Z43-24. Moreover, Z43-16 had the maximum hydrolysis rate and con­
stant, which indicated that it was appropriate to transform the AH 
process to AD at 16 h. In order to overcome the problem of low methane 
production rate of CS, cow manure and chicken manure, Wang indicated 
that mixing the materials could promote the hydrolysis process of AD 
and improve the start-up efficiency of the system (Fuchs et al., 2018; 
Wang et al., 2020b). 
The cumulative methane production reached 202.10 ml/g VS, which 
was lower than that of this study. The main reason is that appropriate 
AH time can effectively degrade the components of lignocellulose, 
provide sufficient nutrition for the initial stage of AD, and increase the 
accessibility of hydrolases to cellulose in the fermentation system (Zhao 
et al., 2019). The analysis of variance for the methane yield was shown 
in supplementary file. The F value and p-value of between groups were 
35.58 and 0.0001, respectively, which indicated that the interaction of 
hydrolysis time on methane yield was significant. Therefore, the 
methane production performance can be significantly improved after 
AH. 
3.3. Degradation of solid organic matter 
Fig. 4 showed the degradation of organic solids and the content of 
methane at the end of AD. With the extension of hydrolysis time, the 
methane content increased first and then decreased, and the maximum 
value appeared at 16 h of hydrolysis, which reached 53.02%. The 
degradation rates of TS and VS of Z43-8, Z43-16 and Z43-24 increased 
gradually with the prolongation of hydrolysis time, which were all 
higher than that of CK. The degradation rates of TS and VS of Z43-16 
were 60.23% and 60.58% respectively, which were 9.43% and 5.25% 
higher than those of CK. It indicated that the utilization rate of CS can be 
improved through AH, and the reason may be that the structure of lignin 
is destroyed during AH. The shielding effect of lignin on cellulose and 
hemicellulose partially disappeared, and the structure of lignocellulose 
of CS became loose, which was more easily used by methanogens 
extracellular enzymes. Aeration of the reaction system in AH stage not 
only increased the dissolved oxygen in the hydrolysate, but also pro­
moted its heat and mass transfer performance. Moreover, the contact 
area between lignocellulose and methanogens was increased, which 
provided sufficient raw materials for the physiological activities of mi­
croorganisms and accelerated the growth and reproduction of metha­
nogens (Wang et al., 2020a). Although the degradation rate of TS and VS 
of Z43-24 was the highest, it can be seen from the previous section that 
the methane production was the highest after 16 h of AH. Therefore, the 
increase of degradation rate of TS and VS did not necessarily improve 
the methane production of the system. AH of CS for 16 h can not only 
improve the degradation rate of TS and VS, but also avoid excessive 
degradation and unnecessary loss.

3.4. Energy consumption analysis 
In this study, a 100 m3 anaerobic reactor was taken as an example. To 
ensure the efficient operation of the reactor, the TS of fermentation 
substrate entering the system was 8%. Based on the Eq. (3) and Eq. (4), 
the heat consumption required for the increase of fermentation raw 
material temperature was shown in supplementary file. According to the 
original design parameters of the reactor, the heat consumption of each 
part of the reactor envelope can be calculated by the Eq. (7)- Eq. (11). 
The monthly heat consumption of AH and AD reactor was shown in 
supplementary file, respectively. 
The calorific value of methane and CS is 890.31 kJ/mol and 17000 
kJ/kg, respectively (Edwiges et al., 2018; Wainaina et al., 2019). In the 
storehouse, the annual temperature difference of raw materials is small, 
so the initial temperature of CS is assumed to be 15 ◦C. The difference 
between the total energy of methane output and the net energy con­
sumption of input system (including raw material crushing, temperature 
increasing, and energy consumption in AH and AD reactor) is defined as 
the theoretical net productivity of the system. The ratio of theoretical 
productivity of each system to the initial total energy of CS is defined as 
energy conversion rate. Moreover, the ratio of theoretical net produc­
tivity of the system to total input net energy consumption is defined as 
embodied energy yield. 
Fig. 5(a) showed the proportion of net energy consumption of AD 
after AH. With the extension of hydrolysis time, the proportion of 
crushing energy consumption fluctuated little, with the maximum of 
Z43-16 (12.93%) and the minimum of Z43-24 (8.47%). The hydrolysis 
energy consumption was the lowest, which was mainly related to the 
hydrolysis time and the monthly average temperature. The proportion of 
energy consumption of heating feed solution and AD was relatively 
large. In the proportion of heating, Z43-16 was the largest with 71% in 
July, and Z43-24 h was the smallest with 32.28% in January. However, 
the initial temperature of raw materials was closely related to the 
environment, so it was not easy to change this proportion. 
The proportion of energy consumption of AD was closely related to 
the fermentation cycle. The maximum was 59.91% in January of Z43-8, 
and the minimum was 14.49% of Z43-16 in July, which mainly due to 
the shorter AD time reachingP90. Elalami mentioned that biochemical 
methane potential (BMP) was not designed to scale up or estimate costs 
of AD system, the effects of any pretreatment were highly dependent on 
the AD process (Elalami et al., 2020). In different AD environment, the 
methanogenic ability of microorganisms is different. For example, 
compared with sequencing batch AD experiment of lignin-like sub­
stances, the hydraulic retention time of continuous AD is shorter, the 
degradation rate of lignocellulose is higher, and its AD system is more 
stable (Velez-Suberbie et al., 2018; Wainaina et al., 2020a). Therefore, 
there are some differences between the performance and net energy 
efficiency of methane production in laboratory scale and actual biogas 
engineering. 
The energy conversion rate of AD after AH was shown in Fig. 5(b). 
From the perspective of hydrolysis time, all conversion rates of Z43-16 
showed good performance, and the peak values of high-quality energy 
yield (445.41%), system energy conversion rate (17.91%), and CS en­
ergy conversion limit (18.66%) all appeared in July, which further 
indicated the hydrolysis effect was the best when AH was carried out to 
16 h. When the temperature was warmed to a certain temperature, the 
raw materials can be better hydrolyzed and mix evenly (Anthraper et al., 
2018; Khan et al., 2019). Therefore, the process of AH for 16 h can 
obtain better comprehensive properties. 
4. Conclusions 
Aerobic hydrolysis can effectively improve the degradation rate of 
lignocellulose. After 24 h of hydrolysis, lignin, cellulose, and hemicel­
lulose of CS were degraded by 8.06%, 27.38%, and 35.73%, respec­
tively. The methane production performance and maximum hydrolysis 
rate and constant were higher when the hydrolysis was carried out for 
16 h. The proportion of energy consumption for crushing and hydrolysis 
was relatively low, while that for heating and AD was relatively high. In 
the biogas engineering, it is suggested that the hydrolysis temperature 
can be controlled at 43 ◦C and transferred to AD at 16 h of AH.
